Note: Aramaic manuscripts of several Enochic works were preserved among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran, confirming the circulation of the Enochic corpus there; the later Book of Parables is not represented.
Multiple Hebrew manuscripts of Jubilees were preserved at Qumran, where its 364-day calendar, angelic revelation, and rewritten patriarchal history closely align with broader sectarian interests.
A Hebrew copy of Ben Sira (2Q18) was found in Qumran Cave 2, demonstrating that the text circulated among the manuscripts preserved at Qumran.

Jubilees reworks Enochic traditions concerning the Watchers, giants, Flood, demons, and revealed knowledge, while integrating them into a Mosaic and Torah-centered history; both also use a 364-day calendar.

The Animal Apocalypse in 1 Enoch symbolically extends Israelite history into the Maccabean revolt, with the great-horned ram commonly identified as Judas Maccabeus; 1 Maccabees narrates the same crisis directly.

Both interpret the Maccabean crisis through divine intervention: 1 Enoch frames it as an apocalyptic cosmic conflict, while 2 Maccabees emphasizes martyrdom, resurrection, angelic aid, and divine judgment.

Both independently narrate the Maccabean revolt, overlapping on Antiochus IV's persecution, the Temple's desecration and purification, Judas Maccabeus, and Nicanor's defeat; 1 Maccabees is dynastic-political, while 2 Maccabees is Jerusalem-centered and theological.
1 Maccabees legitimizes the founding Hasmonean leaders as Israel's liberators, whereas Psalms of Solomon condemns the later Hasmonean rulers as corrupt and anticipates a righteous Davidic king.
